structure: Nine camps on a 3x3 map (economy x culture, each with a centre), split by power into eighteen types. Every type has an average profile on the eight axes; a person or party is aligned with the type whose average profile is closest. Future is a lowercase suffix taken from the person's own scores.

dimensions.name: Economy
dimensions.question: Who should steer the economy: society through the state, markets, or a mix?

dimensions.name: Culture
dimensions.question: Open, plural and free in private life, rooted in tradition, order and national identity, or somewhere in between?

dimensions.name: Power
dimensions.question: Trust shared institutions, experts and alliances, or take power back to the nation and its people?

dimensions.name: Future
dimensions.question: Slow down to protect the planet, or grow and innovate our way forward?

future_notes.e: Leans ecological: willing to accept costs and limits to protect climate and nature, and cautious about new technology.
future_notes.g: Leans towards growth: affordability and innovation come first, and climate rules should not hold the economy back.

camps.name: Progressive centre
camps.summary: A mixed economy and progressive values.

camps.name: Left
camps.summary: Collective economics, in the middle on culture.

camps.name: Centre
camps.summary: In the middle on both the economy and culture.

camps.name: Right
camps.summary: Market economics, in the middle on culture.

camps.name: Conservative centre
camps.summary: A mixed economy and traditional values.

former_note: Former parties are listed for comparison. A type describes policy positions only, not how a party gained or used power.

types.name: The Gardener
types.tagline: Grow a fairer society and a liveable planet, together.
about: Gardeners see society as something you tend together. Good schools, healthcare and public transport give everyone a fair start, and equal rights mean nobody is left out because of who they are or who they love. Climate and nature aren't a side issue: they're the ground everything else grows in.

They believe the big problems of this century don't stop at borders, so they put their trust in cooperation: the EU, international agreements, scientists and experts working on solutions. Patient, well-planned change is how lasting progress is made.

types.name: The Activist
types.tagline: The system works for the few. It's time it worked for everyone.
about: Activists see a world where wealth and power pile up at the top while ordinary people pay the price. They want real change, not tinkering at the edges: fair wages, affordable homes, public ownership of what everyone needs, and equal rights for all.
They don't wait for permission from those in charge. Movements, protests, unions and referendums are how people have won every right they have, and Activists are proud to stand in that tradition.

types.name: The Cosmopolitan
types.tagline: Open to the world, and open-minded at home.
about: Cosmopolitans feel at home in a connected world. They value freedom to live as you choose, to travel, study and work across borders, and they see diversity as a strength. On the economy they're practical: markets where they work, a safety net where they don't.

They believe good decisions come from knowledge and cooperation, which is why they back the EU, international institutions and independent experts. For them, openness is how a country stays prosperous and free.

types.name: The Free Thinker
types.tagline: Live and let live, and keep an eye on anyone with too much power.
about: Free Thinkers care above all about the freedom to think, speak and live as you see fit. They're open-minded on social questions and practical on the economy, and they're quick to notice when governments, corporations or tech platforms start to know or decide too much.
Privacy, free speech and civil liberties are their red lines. They prefer decisions made close to the people they affect, and they trust people more than institutions to work things out.

types.name: The Innovator
types.tagline: Free markets, free people, and a future worth building.
about: Innovators believe in the power of people with ideas. Low taxes, less red tape and open markets give entrepreneurs the room to create jobs and prosperity, and personal freedom applies just as much to how people live their lives.
They're optimistic about technology, from AI to clean energy and medicine, and see a strong rule of law and international cooperation as the foundation that lets innovation flourish.

types.name: The Maverick
types.tagline: Your life, your money, your choice.
about: Mavericks want as much freedom as possible: to keep what you earn, to run your own life and to say what you think. They're relaxed about how other people live, as long as nobody forces their choices on anyone else.
They're sceptical of politicians, central planners and international bodies that make rules from a distance, and they trust free people and free markets to do better than any government.

types.name: The Builder
types.tagline: Decent jobs, affordable homes, and a state that delivers.
about: Builders believe in a society that works for working people. Fair wages, secure jobs, affordable housing and public services that actually function: that's what makes life good, and it's what government is for.
They're practical rather than ideological, and stay out of culture wars. They trust institutions to get things done and measure success in homes built, hospitals open and trains running on time.

types.name: The Organizer
types.tagline: Working people built this country. They deserve their fair share.
about: Organizers stand for solidarity. They want strong unions, fair wages, public ownership of essentials and a welfare state that protects people when times get hard. Ordinary workers, not shareholders or bureaucrats, should come first.
They're wary of elites, distant institutions and trade deals that seem to serve big business more than working communities, and they believe change comes from people organising together.

types.name: The Pragmatist
types.tagline: Look at what works, then do it well.
about: Pragmatists judge every question on its merits. They're comfortable in the middle on the economy and on culture, not out of indecision but because real life rarely fits one ideology. Evidence, experience and common sense guide them.
They value stable institutions, sound government and the art of compromise. To them, a country runs best when people with different views can sit at the same table and find solutions that last.

types.name: The Outsider
types.tagline: Not left, not right. Just a say in how things are run.
about: Outsiders hold practical, middle-of-the-road views, but they've had enough of politics that happens far away from them. They want transparency, honest answers and real influence through referendums and citizens' initiatives.
They look at problems without party glasses. For them, democracy means the people decide, not a closed circle of politicians, lobbyists and officials.

types.name: The Trader
types.tagline: A strong economy is what pays for everything else.
about: Traders believe prosperity comes from enterprise, open markets and sound public finances. Lower taxes, fewer rules and free trade let businesses grow, and a growing economy is what funds good public services.
They take a moderate line on social questions and value reliable institutions, international agreements and a government that keeps its books in order.

types.name: The Independent
types.tagline: Let people run their own lives, and their own businesses.
about: Independents value self-reliance. Many work for themselves or run a small business, and they know what it takes. They want lower taxes, fewer rules and decisions made close to home.

They're broadly tolerant on social questions but want a clear say over who comes into the country and how it's run. They trust their own judgement more than that of politicians and distant institutions.

types.name: The Steward
types.tagline: Care for your neighbour, and for the world we hold in trust.
about: Stewards combine a strong social conscience with traditional values, often rooted in faith. They want a society that protects the vulnerable, supports families and treats life with care, from beginning to end.
They see protecting nature as a moral duty and value cooperation, institutions and the rule of law. For Stewards, community and responsibility matter more than individual gain.

types.name: The Tribune
types.tagline: Look after your own people first.
about: Tribunes stand up for working people and the communities they come from. They want secure jobs, good pensions and public services, and they want their country to stay recognisably theirs, with control over migration and over its own decisions.
They distrust a political class that seems to have forgotten ordinary people, and believe a nation's first duty is to its own citizens.

types.name: The Neighbour
types.tagline: Family, community and a steady hand on the wheel.
about: Neighbours value the things that hold a society together: family, community, tradition and shared norms. They support a social market economy where hard work is rewarded and nobody falls through the cracks.
They trust institutions, alliances and the rule of law, and prefer careful, responsible government to grand experiments. Stability, for them, is something to protect.

types.name: The Homesteader
types.tagline: Our land, our traditions, and our say over both.
about: Homesteaders are rooted in their country, its culture and its countryside. They want to protect a way of life that took generations to build, with strong families, local communities and much more control over migration.
They believe decisions about a country belong to its own people, not to distant institutions, and they're proud to stand up for that.

types.name: The Statesman
about: Statesmen believe in a strong economy, safe streets and a country that keeps its word. Moderate taxes and enterprise create prosperity; law and order and controlled migration keep society stable.
They value tradition, strong institutions and firm alliances, and prefer steady, responsible government to grand gestures. Leadership, for them, means getting the basics right.

types.name: The Challenger
types.tagline: Take back control of the borders, the money and the country.
about: Challengers want their country back in the hands of its people. They stand for secure borders, lower taxes, affordable energy and pride in national identity and tradition.

They're not afraid to take on the political establishment, international bodies or the media when they think those have stopped listening, and they see themselves as the voice of people who were ignored for too long.

alignment.note: Climate and technology count half, because they are shown separately as the small letter.
